title: The history of the pen
tagline: 5,000 years from a sharpened reed to a ball that rolls ink.
intro: For most of history, writing meant dipping a sharpened stick or feather in ink every few words. Scribes in Egypt and Greece cut reeds, Europe wrote with goose feathers for a thousand years, and a Fatimid caliph asked for a pen that held its own ink. Then steel nibs, the fountain pen and, in the 1930s, a Hungarian journalist's rolling ball put a cheap, reliable pen in every pocket.

eras.name: Reeds, brushes and feathers
eras.summary: Writing means dipping. Reeds, brushes and quills carry a little ink from a pot to the page, and paper arrives from China.

eras.name: Steel nibs and fountain pens
eras.summary: Machines stamp out steel nibs by the million, and inventors finally make a pen that carries its own ink without leaking.

eras.name: The ballpoint revolution
eras.summary: A rolling ball and thick, fast-drying ink make the first pen that almost anyone can afford and nobody needs to refill.

eras.name: Markers, gels and screens
eras.summary: Felt tips, rollerballs, gel ink, erasable ink and pens that write on glass.

events.title: Rush pens and soot ink
events.text: Egyptian scribes wrote on papyrus with thin rushes chewed or cut into a brush-like tip, dipped in ink made from soot (carbon) bound with plant gum.
events.why: Carbon ink is so stable that texts written with it thousands of years ago are still black today.

events.title: The split reed pen
events.text: Scribes cut a hard reed (in Greek, kalamos) to a point and split its tip, so the ink ran down the split to the paper as they wrote.
events.why: A slit that feeds ink to a point is the ancestor of every pen nib.

events.title: Paper
events.text: Cai Lun, an official of the Han court, is credited with improving and standardising papermaking from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets. Paper spread along the Silk Road to the Islamic world and, much later, to Europe.
events.why: Pens are only half the story: cheap paper made writing an everyday act.

events.title: The quill
events.text: Flight feathers, usually from geese, became Europe's main writing tool. The hollow shaft held a small drop of ink, and a penknife recut the point as it wore down. Isidore of Seville mentions quills in the early 600s.
events.why: The quill wrote most of Europe's books, letters and laws for over a thousand years. The word “pen” comes from the Latin penna, feather.

events.title: A pen that holds its own ink
events.text: The Fatimid caliph asked for a pen that wouldn't stain his hands or clothes. According to his chronicler, Qadi al-Nu'man, he was given a pen that carried ink in a reservoir and let it out only when used for writing.
events.why: It is the earliest known record of what we'd now call a fountain pen.

events.title: Iron gall ink
events.text: Ink made from oak galls and iron salts turns from pale to deep black as it reacts with air, and bites into parchment so it can't be scraped off. It was the standard ink for centuries.
events.why: Many of the most important documents in Western history are written in it, but its acidity slowly eats the page.

events.title: Two quills, one reservoir
events.text: Schwenter described a pen made from two quills, one inside the other. The inner quill held ink, sealed with a cork, and fed it to the writing point.
events.why: An early European attempt at a pen that doesn't need dipping.

events.title: Machine-made steel nibs
events.who: John Mitchell, Josiah Mason, Joseph Gillott and others
events.text: Birmingham factories began stamping nibs out of sheet steel by machine. By the mid-1800s the city made more than half of the world's pens.
events.why: A cheap, long-lasting nib replaced the quill and brought writing to schools and offices everywhere.

events.title: A patent for a self-feeding pen
events.text: Poenaru, a Romanian inventor studying in Paris, was granted a French patent for a pen that fed itself from a reservoir made from a large swan quill.
events.why: One of the first patented fountain pens.

events.title: A feed that stops blots
events.text: Waterman patented a feed with fine channels that let ink out by capillary action while letting air in, so the pen stopped blotting. The popular story that a leaking pen cost him a contract may be a legend.
events.why: Balancing ink out and air in is still how every fountain pen works.

events.title: The first ballpoint patent
events.text: Loud, a leather tanner, patented a pen with a small rotating steel ball held in a socket, for marking rough surfaces like leather. It was too coarse for writing letters and the patent lapsed.
events.why: The rolling ball worked, but the right ink was still fifty years away.

events.title: Handwriting sent down a wire
events.text: Gray's telautograph used a pen connected to linkages that turned its movements into electrical signals. A second pen, miles away, copied the writing as it happened.
events.why: An ancestor of the fax machine and of the digital stylus.

events.title: Refill with a lever
events.text: Sheaffer patented a fountain pen with a lever on the side. Flip it and it squeezed a rubber ink sac inside; let go and the sac drew in fresh ink from a bottle.
events.why: No more eyedroppers: filling a pen became clean and quick.

events.title: The Bíró brothers' ballpoint
events.text: László Bíró, a journalist, noticed that newspaper ink dried fast without smudging, but was too thick for a fountain pen. With his brother György, a chemist, he paired thick, quick-drying ink with a ball in a socket and patented it in Britain.
events.why: The right ink made the rolling ball practical. In many countries a ballpoint is still called a “biro”.

events.title: Made in Argentina
events.text: Fleeing the war in Europe, the brothers settled in Argentina, filed a new patent and began making “Birome” pens. Argentina celebrates Inventor's Day on 29 September, László Bíró's birthday.
events.why: The ballpoint's first commercial home was in South America.

events.title: Pens that work at altitude
events.text: The British government licensed Bíró's design so RAF aircrew could write in unpressurised planes, where fountain pens leaked as the air pressure dropped.
events.why: A war-time need proved the ballpoint was tougher than the fountain pen.

events.title: The Reynolds Rocket goes on sale
events.text: American businessman Milton Reynolds rushed out a ballpoint and sold it at Gimbels department store for $12.50, a lot of money at the time. Crowds queued and thousands sold on the first day, though many early pens leaked or skipped.
events.why: It showed the enormous demand for a pen you never had to dip or fill.

events.title: The Bic Cristal
events.text: Bich bought rights to Bíró's design and used Swiss watchmaking machines to make precise balls cheaply. The Cristal's clear hexagonal barrel shows the ink left, and a tiny hole in the barrel equalises air pressure.
events.why: Bic says it has sold more than 100 billion Cristals: the pen became disposable.

events.title: The Magic Marker
events.text: Rosenthal's marker was a glass bottle of ink with a wool-felt wick that drew ink up to the tip by capillary action.
events.why: Bold, quick-drying lines on almost any surface: the start of the felt-tip.

events.title: The fibre-tip pen
events.text: Horie developed a pen with a tip made of bundled acrylic fibres, fed by capillary action from a water-based ink reservoir. The Pentel Sign Pen became hugely popular.
events.why: The ancestor of today's felt-tips, fineliners and whiteboard markers.

events.title: The rollerball
events.text: Ohto paired a ballpoint's rolling ball with thin, water-based ink, giving a smooth, wet line like a fountain pen's.
events.why: Same ball, different ink: the ink's thickness changes everything about how a pen writes.

events.title: The space pen
events.text: Fisher patented a sealed refill with pressurised nitrogen behind the ink, so it writes upside down, underwater and in weightlessness. Astronauts used it from Apollo 7 in 1968. The popular tale that NASA spent millions on it while Soviet cosmonauts used pencils is a myth: Fisher paid for its development.
events.why: It solved the ballpoint's dependence on gravity.

events.title: The gel pen
events.text: Sakura launched a ballpoint using gel ink: water-based ink thickened with a polymer that flows when the ball turns and thickens again at rest.
events.why: Vivid, opaque colours, including metallics and pastels, that ordinary ballpoint ink can't carry.

events.title: Ink that disappears
events.text: Pilot's FriXion pens use thermosensitive ink that turns clear when warmed. Rubbing with the pen's rubber tip makes enough heat from friction to erase it.
events.why: A new trick for an old tool, from chemistry rather than mechanics.

events.title: The pen goes digital
events.text: Pressure- and tilt-sensitive styluses, such as the Apple Pencil (2015), let tablets record handwriting and drawing with the feel of a real pen.
events.why: Gray's 1888 idea, finally in everyone's hands: writing that becomes data.

firsts.label: A pen holding its own ink

people.name: Cai Lun
people.note: Credited with improving papermaking in 105 CE.

people.name: Petrache Poenaru
people.note: Patented an early self-feeding fountain pen in Paris.

people.name: Lewis Waterman
people.note: Patented a feed that balanced ink out and air in.

people.name: Elisha Gray
people.note: Invented the telautograph, which sent handwriting down a wire.

people.name: John J. Loud
people.note: Patented the first ballpoint pen in 1888.

people.name: László Bíró
people.note: With his brother György, made the first practical ballpoint.

people.name: Milton Reynolds
people.note: Sold the first ballpoints in the United States.

people.name: Marcel Bich
people.note: Created the Bic Cristal, the best-selling pen in history.

facts: The word “pen” comes from the Latin penna, which means feather.
In many countries a ballpoint is still called a “biro”, after László Bíró.
Argentina celebrates Inventor's Day on 29 September, Bíró's birthday.
RAF aircrew were among the first to use ballpoints, because fountain pens leaked at altitude.
The story that NASA spent millions on a space pen while cosmonauts used pencils is a myth.
